title: fix: scroll offset_x by visual width, not char count, in focus()
body:
## Summary
- `Editor::focus()` decided whether to scroll horizontally by comparing the cursor's raw character-count column against the viewport width, which under-counts the true display width of lines containing double-width glyphs (CJK, emoji). This could leave the cursor off-screen while `focus()` believed no scroll was needed, disagreeing with `get_visible_cursor()`, which already accounts for grapheme display width.
- `focus()` now computes the cursor's and `offset_x`'s visual columns the same way `get_visible_cursor()` does (summing grapheme widths), and resolves scroll targets back to a character index via a new `char_idx_for_visual_col()` helper.

Fixes #15

## Test plan
- [x] Added `focus_scrolls_horizontally_for_wide_glyph_lines` in `tests/input.rs`, reproducing the issue's repro case (a 20-character line of `界`, 40-cell-wide viewport) — cursor now stays visible after `focus()`.
- [x] `cargo test` (33 tests across lib + integration suites) passes.
- [x] `cargo clippy --all-targets` shows no new warnings from this change.

title: focus() doesn't scroll horizontally for wide-glyph lines, leaving the cursor off-screen
Feature-gate Tree-sitter language support
body:
## Problem

`ratatui-code-editor` currently includes every supported Tree-sitter grammar as an unconditional dependency. This is convenient for general-purpose editors, but it makes the crate heavier for consumers that only need one or a small number of languages.

For example, I’m evaluating `ratatui-code-editor` for a terminal-native application whose embedded editor only needs Lua. Today, depending on the crate also pulls in the grammars for Rust, JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Go, Java, C, C++, HTML, CSS, C#, YAML, JSON, TOML, Bash, Markdown, etc.

Would you be open to feature-gating language support so consumers can opt into only the grammars they need?

## Proposed shape

One possible approach would be:

```toml
[dependencies]
tree-sitter-rust = { version = "...", optional = true }
tree-sitter-javascript = { version = "...", optional = true }
# ...

[features]
default = ["crossterm", "all-languages"]

language-rust = ["dep:tree-sitter-rust"]
language-javascript = ["dep:tree-sitter-javascript"]
# ...

all-languages = [
    "language-rust",
    "language-javascript",
    # ...
]
```

The corresponding entries in `Code::get_language()` could then be guarded with `#[cfg(feature = "language-...")]`.

Keeping `all-languages` in the default feature set would preserve the current behavior for existing users, while allowing downstream consumers to do something like:

```toml
ratatui-code-editor = {
    version = "...",
    default-features = false,
    features = ["crossterm", "language-lua"]
}
```

## Lua use case

Lua is the immediate language I need. I noticed the repository already contains `langs/lua/highlights.scm`, but Lua is not currently wired into `Code::get_language()` and there is no Lua Tree-sitter grammar dependency in `Cargo.toml`.

My thought would be to keep this change small and split the work into two PRs:

1. Feature-gate the existing language dependencies without changing supported-language behavior.
2. Add Lua support as a follow-up using the same feature structure.

That would make the first PR primarily a packaging/API change and keep Lua support independently reviewable.

## Open questions

Before putting together a PR, I’d like your preference on a few details:

* Does one feature per language seem like the right API?
* Should all currently supported languages remain enabled by default for backward compatibility?
* Would you prefer names like `language-rust` / `language-lua`, or simply `rust` / `lua`?
* Is it worth feature-gating the embedded `langs/*` query assets as well, or is gating the parser dependencies sufficient for a first pass?

I’d be happy to put together the implementation if this direction makes sense.

body:
Hello!

Thank you for this lib, it looks really great :)

I was wondering if vim-like mode and key bindings are going to be supported?
I really want to replace rhysd's [tui-textarea](https://github.com/rhysd/tui-textarea) by yours in [ATAC](https://github.com/Julien-cpsn/ATAC) because it is not very flexible and does not support syntax highlighting, but the blocking point for yours is the support of vim/emacs mode which is really great in his lib but abstent here.

Don't get me wrong, I just genuinly think that it could be a great feature!

Have a great day
